title: How a Georgia Factory Solved Its Worker Shortage by Ditching the 40-Hour Week
summary: In the rolling hills of northwest Georgia, a quiet revolution is reshaping factory work. The Roper Corporation, a GE Appliances plant that churns out ovens and ranges, was drowning in orders during the pandemic—and hemorrhaging workers. On some days, the factory was hundreds of employees short. Salaried staff, including the plant director, had to jump onto the assembly line to keep production moving. The solution? Blow up the traditional 40-hour, show-up-every-day model. Plant leaders, after some initial skepticism, introduced four-hour shifts that workers could pick up through the MyWorkChoice app. The move was radical for an industry built on consistency and predictability. But it worked. Today, about 450 flexible workers—roughly half the available pool—sign up for shifts each week, averaging 24 hours. Their contributions were crucial to a $180 million plant expansion that added 600 jobs. For people like 68-year-old Ruth Ransom, who wanted only a few days of work to stay active, the flexibility is a perfect fit. The experiment shows that even in heavy manufacturing, giving workers control over their schedules can solve deep labor shortages.
why_it_matters: If this experiment scales, it could redefine factory work for millions, challenging a century-old model that treats workers as interchangeable parts. It suggests that addressing worker dignity and autonomy may be key to reviving U.S. manufacturing.

background_read: The Roper Corporation is a subsidiary of Haier, a Chinese appliance giant, and makes GE-branded ovens. The factory's crisis occurred during the COVID-19 pandemic, which triggered the 'Great Resignation'—a period when millions of workers quit jobs across the U.S., especially in manufacturing, retail, and hospitality. Traditional factories have long relied on fixed 8-hour shifts and strict attendance, a model inherited from the Industrial Revolution. The MyWorkChoice app used at Roper is part of a broader gig-economy trend that has reshaped other industries like ride-sharing (Uber) and food delivery (DoorDash), but it is rare in heavy manufacturing. The $180 million expansion added 600 permanent jobs, suggesting that flexibility and growth can go hand in hand. The experience is being watched by other manufacturers struggling with the same labor crunch.

perspectives.description: Workers gain the flexibility to balance jobs with family, school, or retirement, while the company fills shifts it desperately needed. The plant's growth shows that flexibility can coexist with heavy industry, potentially attracting people who would otherwise avoid factory work.

Flexible shifts may mean less income security for workers who rely on hours that can vary week to week, without benefits tied to full-time status. Critics argue this is a band-aid—wages and conditions, not just schedule control, must improve to really solve labor shortages.

The Roper case fits a larger pattern: as the workforce ages and younger generations demand more autonomy, manufacturing must adapt or perish. Historically, production lines were designed for efficiency through uniformity, but the rise of app-based scheduling could fragment the workforce and reshape labor laws.

If more factories adopt this model, policymakers may need to create portable benefit systems for non-traditional shifts, and unions might negotiate for guaranteed minimum hours alongside flexibility. The experiment could also push automation, as companies seek even more flexible production methods.
